name: Pager
blurb: A belt-clip beeper that showed a callback number; you replied from a payphone
title: What Was a Pager? How Beepers Worked, Codes and Who Uses Them
description: A pager, or beeper, was a small receiver that beeped and showed a number or short text. Big in the 1990s, replaced by mobile phones, still in some hospitals.
answer: A pager, or beeper, was a small receive-only radio device, usually clipped to a belt, that beeped when someone paged you and showed the phone number to call back, or later a short text. Pagers were everywhere in the 1990s as a cheaper alternative to mobile phones, then faded fast as phones and text messaging spread. Consumer paging has shut down in most countries, but pagers are still used in some hospitals and emergency services.

body: To reach someone, you called their paging number (or an operator) and keyed in your own phone number. Their pager beeped or vibrated and showed the digits. Because the pager could not make calls, they then had to find a payphone or a landline to call you back.

Early devices only beeped; numeric pagers showed digits; alphanumeric pagers could show a short text message. Some services also let callers leave a voice message that the pager owner had to dial in to hear.
With only digits on the screen, people invented codes:

ul: 143: "I love you", counting the letters in each word
07734: "hello", read with the pager held upside down
-911 added after a number: call back right now
520 in China: "I love you", because wǔ èr líng sounds like wǒ ài nǐ

body: Yes, in niches. Some hospitals and emergency services keep them because they are seen as simple and reliable for urgent calls; the UK's NHS was still using roughly 130,000 pagers when it announced plans to phase them out. Restaurants use simple coaster-style pagers to tell you your table is ready. A paging service still runs in Hong Kong. For everyone else, pagers are now collector items.

faq.q: Could you call someone from a pager?
faq.a: No. Classic pagers only received; you replied from a payphone or landline. Later two-way pagers could send short replies.

faq.q: What did 143 mean on a pager?
faq.a: "I love you", from the number of letters in I (1), love (4) and you (3).

faq.q: Why do hospitals still use pagers?
faq.a: They are simple and seen as reliable for urgent alerts, although some health services, such as the UK's NHS, have announced plans to phase them out.
